questions.q: A 28-year-old man from rural India presents with a single hypopigmented anaesthetic patch on the forearm, present for 8 months. Slit-skin smear is negative. Histopathology shows well-formed granulomas with lymphocytes surrounding nerve bundles. What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.exp: Tuberculoid leprosy presents with a single well-defined anaesthetic patch, negative slit-skin smear (paucibacillary), and histology showing well-formed epithelioid granulomas with lymphocytes eroding the perineurium — classic features of TT. BT has more lesions with slight variation in morphology.

questions.q: A 35-year-old HIV-positive male presents with multiple satellite lesions around a primary plaque on the gluteal area. KOH mount shows thick-walled budding yeast cells with a broad-based bud. What is the most likely causative organism?
questions.exp: Blastomyces dermatitidis produces thick-walled yeast cells with a characteristic broad-based single bud ('figure-of-8' appearance on KOH mount). The broad base distinguishes it from Cryptococcus (narrow-based budding) and Candida (pseudohyphae).

questions.q: A 22-year-old woman presents with painless vulval ulcer with clean base and indurated edges. VDRL is non-reactive. Darkfield microscopy shows spirochetes. What is the most appropriate next step in management?
questions.exp: Primary syphilis with darkfield-confirmed Treponema pallidum is treated with Benzathine penicillin 2.4 MU IM as a single dose. VDRL may be non-reactive in early primary syphilis due to the immunological window period.

questions.q: A patient on long-term phenytoin develops generalised skin thickening, coarse facial features, and hypertrichosis. Which condition does this phenytoin-induced skin change most closely mimic?
questions.exp: Long-term phenytoin can cause a pachydermoperiostosis-like syndrome with thickened skin, coarse features, and periosteal changes. Phenytoin also causes gingival hyperplasia and hypertrichosis.

questions.q: A 40-year-old woman develops bullae on sun-exposed areas. Immunofluorescence shows IgG deposits at the dermo-epidermal junction. Immunoelectron microscopy localises deposits below the lamina densa. Which is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.exp: EBA is characterised by IgG (rarely IgA) autoantibodies against type VII collagen, which is situated in the anchoring fibrils below the lamina densa. DIF shows IgG at the DEJ (u-serrated pattern). BP deposits are above the lamina densa (in the lamina lucida).

questions.q: A 55-year-old male smoker presents with a solitary firm, pearly papule with telangiectasias on the nose, present for 2 years. It has recently developed a central ulcer. What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.exp: Nodular basal cell carcinoma classically presents as a pearly papule or nodule with rolled edges, telangiectasias, and central ulceration (rodent ulcer). It is the most common skin cancer, occurring predominantly on sun-exposed areas of the head and neck.

questions.q: A 30-year-old woman with butterfly rash and joint pain has a positive ANA. Which antibody is most specific for systemic lupus erythematosus and correlates with disease activity?
questions.exp: Anti-dsDNA antibodies are highly specific for SLE and titres correlate with disease activity, particularly lupus nephritis. Anti-Sm is highly specific but does not correlate with activity. Anti-histone is associated with drug-induced lupus.

questions.q: A neonate presents at birth with generalised blistering, dystrophic nails, and milia formation. Electron microscopy shows cleavage at the level of the sub-lamina densa with absent anchoring fibrils. Which type of epidermolysis bullosa is most likely?
questions.exp: Dystrophic EB (recessive, Hallopeau-Siemens) is caused by mutations in COL7A1 (type VII collagen). Cleavage is sub-lamina densa with absent/rudimentary anchoring fibrils on EM. Features include scarring, milia, nail dystrophy, and oesophageal strictures.

questions.q: A 45-year-old patient presents with Wickham's striae on the buccal mucosa and violaceous flat-topped papules on the flexor wrists. Which cell type mediates the band-like lymphocytic infiltrate seen in lichen planus?
questions.exp: Lichen planus is a T-cell-mediated autoimmune condition. CD8+ cytotoxic T lymphocytes form the band-like lichenoid infiltrate in the upper dermis, targeting basal keratinocytes (which may express altered MHC class I), leading to vacuolar degeneration and civatte bodies.

questions.q: A 25-year-old presents with grouped vesicles on the elbow and knees with intense pruritus. DIF shows granular IgA deposits in dermal papillae. What is the most appropriate treatment?
questions.exp: Dermatitis herpetiformis is characterised by granular IgA deposits in dermal papillae on DIF and is strongly associated with gluten-sensitive enteropathy. Dapsone provides rapid symptomatic relief; gluten-free diet is the definitive long-term treatment.

questions.q: A 50-year-old man presents with a 4-month history of painless lymphadenopathy and multiple reddish-brown nodules on the skin. Histopathology shows a spindle cell tumour with slit-like vascular spaces and a background inflammatory infiltrate. HHV-8 serology is positive. What is the diagnosis?
questions.exp: Kaposi's sarcoma is caused by HHV-8 (KSHV) and is strongly associated with HIV/AIDS. Histology shows spindle cells, slit-like vascular channels, extravasated erythrocytes, and plasma cells. HHV-8 latent nuclear antigen (LANA-1) is detected by immunohistochemistry.

questions.q: A 32-year-old woman presents with Raynaud's phenomenon, sclerodactyly, and calcinosis. Anti-centromere antibody is positive. What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.exp: Anti-centromere antibodies are strongly associated with limited systemic sclerosis (formerly CREST syndrome: Calcinosis, Raynaud's, Oesophageal dysmotility, Sclerodactyly, Telangiectasias). Diffuse SSc is associated with anti-Scl-70 (anti-topoisomerase I).

questions.q: A 6-year-old child presents with honey-coloured crusted lesions on the face. Culture grows Staphylococcus aureus. What is the toxin responsible if the child develops bullous lesions with Nikolsky sign?
questions.exp: Staphylococcal scalded skin syndrome (SSSS) and bullous impetigo are caused by exfoliative toxins A and B (ET-A is encoded chromosomally; ET-B is plasmid-encoded). These toxins are serine proteases that cleave desmoglein-1, causing intra-epidermal cleavage in the granular layer.

questions.q: A 19-year-old presents with multiple comedones, inflammatory papules, and pustules on the face and back. He is started on oral isotretinoin. Which monitoring parameter is most critical during the first month of therapy?
opts: Fasting lipid profile and liver function tests
questions.exp: Isotretinoin can cause hypertriglyceridaemia, hypercholesterolaemia, and elevated liver enzymes (transaminases). Baseline and monthly fasting lipid profiles and LFTs are mandatory. Triglycerides >500 mg/dL warrant dose reduction or discontinuation due to pancreatitis risk.

questions.q: A 28-year-old man presents with a painless, non-tender inguinal lymphadenopathy (bubo). Aspirate from the node reveals gram-negative organisms in 'school of fish' pattern. What is the causative organism?
questions.exp: Lymphogranuloma venereum (LGV) is caused by Chlamydia trachomatis serovars L1, L2, L3. The classical presentation is a painless primary genital ulcer followed by painful inguinal bubo. Haemophilus ducreyi (chancroid) causes painful ulcer and tender bubo; 'school of fish' is specifically Haemophilus on Gram stain.

questions.q: A dermatologist performs a Tzanck smear from the floor of a fresh vesicle. The smear shows multinucleated giant cells with steel-grey nuclei and nuclear moulding. This finding is characteristic of which condition?
questions.exp: Tzanck smear showing multinucleated giant cells (Tzanck cells/Touton giant cells) with nuclear moulding is characteristic of herpes group virus infections (HSV-1, HSV-2, VZV). Pemphigus shows acantholytic cells (Tzanck cells of pemphigus), not giant cells.

questions.q: A 60-year-old woman presents with well-demarcated erythematous plaques with silvery scales over the extensor surfaces. She is started on methotrexate. Which folate-mediated enzyme is inhibited by methotrexate?
questions.exp: Methotrexate inhibits dihydrofolate reductase (DHFR), preventing conversion of dihydrofolate to tetrahydrofolate, thereby inhibiting purine and pyrimidine synthesis and reducing T-cell proliferation. Folic acid supplementation reduces side effects without significantly reducing efficacy.

questions.q: A 35-year-old atopic woman presents with intensely pruritic, lichenified plaques in the antecubital and popliteal fossae. Patch testing is negative. Her serum IgE level is markedly elevated. Which cytokines are primarily responsible for the IgE switch in atopic dermatitis?
questions.exp: IL-4 and IL-13 are key Th2 cytokines that drive IgE class switching in B cells via STAT6 signalling. They also downregulate epidermal barrier proteins (filaggrin, loricrin). Dupilumab, a monoclonal antibody targeting the shared IL-4Rα subunit, blocks both IL-4 and IL-13 signalling.

questions.q: A patient with borderline leprosy develops painful erythematous oedematous plaques with fever and constitutional symptoms. Nerve tenderness is noted. This reaction is NOT seen in which type of leprosy?
questions.exp: Type 1 (reversal) reaction is a delayed-type hypersensitivity reaction occurring across the borderline spectrum (BT, BB, BL) and is characterised by acute inflammation of existing lesions and nerves. It does NOT occur in polar tuberculoid (TT) or polar lepromatous (LL) leprosy. Type 2 (ENL) occurs in BL and LL.

questions.q: A 25-year-old woman presents with depigmented macules on the dorsum of hands and perioral area. Wood's lamp examination shows enhanced depigmentation. She is positive for anti-melanocyte antibodies. Which HLA type is most strongly associated with this condition?
questions.exp: Vitiligo has the strongest HLA association with HLA-A2, which is also associated with Addison's disease and other autoimmune conditions. The autoimmune hypothesis is supported by presence of anti-melanocyte antibodies (anti-tyrosinase) and association with other autoimmune diseases.

questions.q: A 42-year-old man presents with targetoid skin lesions (target lesions) on the palms and soles along with erosions on the oral mucosa. He had started co-trimoxazole 2 weeks ago. What is the most appropriate immediate management?
opts: Continue co-trimoxazole and add oral prednisolone
Stop co-trimoxazole and provide supportive care
Switch to dapsone and add cyclosporine
questions.exp: This presentation is consistent with Stevens-Johnson syndrome (SJS) triggered by co-trimoxazole — the most common drug cause. The foremost step is immediate withdrawal of the offending drug. Supportive care (wound care, fluid balance, eye care) is the mainstay. IVIG or cyclosporine may be considered in severe cases after drug withdrawal.

questions.q: A 50-year-old immunocompromised patient develops reactivation of VZV. He presents with vesicles in a dermatomal distribution on the thorax. Which antiviral, given within 72 hours, most effectively reduces the duration and severity of postherpetic neuralgia?
questions.exp: Valacyclovir (prodrug of acyclovir) achieves higher plasma levels, requiring three times daily dosing versus five times for acyclovir. It significantly reduces the duration of postherpetic neuralgia when started within 72 hours of rash onset. Famciclovir is an alternative. Foscarnet is reserved for acyclovir-resistant VZV.

questions.q: In Mohs micrographic surgery, which type of tissue sectioning allows examination of 100% of surgical margins?
questions.exp: Mohs surgery uses horizontal (en face) sectioning of the excised tissue, which allows examination of the entire peripheral and deep margins (nearly 100%). Traditional bread-loaf (vertical) sectioning samples only 0.1% of margins, missing subclinical tumour extensions.

questions.q: A 38-year-old male presents with punched-out ulcers with undermined edges on the lower limbs. The ulcers started as tender pustules. He has a history of Crohn's disease. Pathergy test is positive. What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.exp: Pyoderma gangrenosum is a neutrophilic dermatosis characterised by rapidly progressive painful ulcers with undermined, violaceous edges, beginning as pustules. It is strongly associated with IBD (Crohn's, UC), RA, and haematological malignancies. Pathergy (lesion induction at trauma sites) is a feature.

questions.q: A 16-year-old girl presents with multiple firm, skin-coloured papules on the upper trunk and arms. Histology shows a proliferation of spindle-shaped melanocytes arranged in fascicles within the dermis, with uniform nuclei and no mitoses. What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.exp: Intradermal melanocytic naevi are common benign lesions. Histology shows mature-appearing melanocytes (naevus cells) arranged in nests in the dermis, with no junctional component, no atypia, and no mitotic activity. Blue naevus has heavily pigmented dendritic melanocytes in the mid-dermis.

questions.q: A 60-year-old man develops tender, erythematous nodules on the shins bilaterally. Biopsy shows septal panniculitis without vasculitis. He recently started anti-TB therapy. Which drug is the most common cause of erythema nodosum in this scenario?
questions.exp: Pyrazinamide (PZA) is the most common anti-TB drug associated with erythema nodosum, though the TB infection itself may also be a cause. PZA inhibits uric acid excretion, causing hyperuricaemia; it also has immunological effects. Rifampicin causes other cutaneous reactions (flushing, orange discolouration).

questions.q: A 24-year-old man presents with recurrent oral aphthous ulcers, genital ulcers, and hypopyon uveitis. He is from Turkey. Pathergy test is positive. Which criterion is pathognomonic for this condition in the ISG criteria?
questions.exp: In the International Study Group (ISG) criteria for Behçet's disease, recurrent oral ulceration (at least 3 episodes in 12 months) is the mandatory/pathognomonic criterion. The diagnosis requires oral ulceration PLUS at least 2 of: genital ulceration, skin lesions, eye lesions, or positive pathergy test.

questions.q: A 33-year-old man presents with annular plaques with central clearing on the trunk. Skin scraping KOH preparation shows fungal hyphae. He has been applying a topical steroid for 4 weeks, leading to 'tinea incognito.' Which fungal element is most commonly involved in tinea corporis?
questions.exp: Trichophyton rubrum is the most common dermatophyte worldwide causing tinea corporis (and most other superficial dermatophytoses). It produces ectothrix infection. Tinea incognito results from inappropriate steroid use masking classical features, making the infection more extensive and atypical.

questions.q: A 55-year-old woman presents with photosensitivity, heliotrope rash, Gottron's papules, and proximal muscle weakness. Creatine kinase is elevated. Which malignancy is most commonly associated with dermatomyositis in adults above 50 years of age?
questions.exp: Dermatomyositis in adults over 50 is associated with malignancy in 15-30% of cases. In women, ovarian cancer is the most common associated malignancy. In men, lung and gastrointestinal cancers are more common. All newly diagnosed adult DM patients should undergo age-appropriate malignancy screening.

questions.q: A patient with lepromatous leprosy develops painful nodular erythematous eruptions with fever, joint pain, and iritis. His bacterial index is 5+. This type of reaction is mediated by which immunological mechanism?
questions.exp: Erythema nodosum leprosum (ENL, Type 2 reaction) occurs in BL and LL leprosy. It is mediated by immune complex deposition (Type III hypersensitivity), with complement activation and neutrophil infiltration. Type 1 (reversal) reaction is Type IV (cell-mediated). TNF-α plays a key role in ENL, explaining thalidomide's efficacy.
